Client Work · via ProSense

Salad · Adelanto de Nómina

A payroll-advance acquisition flow for Novacard's Mexican market, delivered through ProSense. Shipped in one month against a three-to-six-month estimate, then proven with a live four-variant test on paid traffic.

Product Manager Novacard · via ProSense Aug 2026 · 1 month Visit the live page ↗

The Problem

Payroll advance is a category where the decision takes minutes and trust is the only real barrier. The Mexican market already had minu.mx and platacard.mx competing on speed, with Dave, Brigit and EarnIn setting user expectations globally. Novacard needed an acquisition flow that converted cold, paid traffic into completed applications without the user ever speaking to a human.

My Role

Product manager, owning the product end to end: wrote the PRD from scratch through structured stakeholder interviews, directed the design with written rationale for each decision, built the prototypes on the existing design system, and ran the post-launch analytics myself.

Constraints That Shaped The Design

  • Advance capped at 10,000 MXN: determined how the calculator framed the offer
  • LFPDPPP, Mexico's data protection law: governed what the form could ask and how consent was captured
  • Full attribution required end to end: UTM and click_id, with an affiliate route on AppsFlyer OneLink using dynamic click_id injection
  • Multi-team scope with external integrations, originally scoped at three to six months

Decisions & Why

The flow runs hero → calculator → form, deliberately in that order: the user sees their own number before being asked for any data.

I chose the variant that puts real app screens inside the "how it works" section, in a category where the fear is "will the money actually arrive," showing the product removes uncertainty before the user commits their details. The final screen carries the same logic: a funds-received notification, not a generic confirmation.

A real customer testimonial replaced a stock crowd photo. Trust in fintech is built on people, not imagery. And a scenario line sits above the headline so the user recognizes their own situation before reading the offer. The Adelanto de Nómina card is also visually prioritized in the "Why Nova" block, above.

Result

Shipped in one month against a three-to-six-month estimate. Four landing page variants ran live on paid traffic from launch. In the first 11 days:

Variant Visits Started Completed Conversion
/391,73848028416.3%
/491,42938323016.1%
/791,46948127919.0%
/991,53947628718.6%
Total6,1751,8201,08017.5%

The best-performing variant converted at 19.0% against 16.1% for the weakest, an 18% relative lift on identical paid traffic, found by testing rather than guessing.

17.5% of paid visits converted to a completed application, well above the 2–5% typical benchmark for cold fintech lead generation. 59.3% of everyone who started the form finished it, directly downstream of the trust decisions above: the product preview, the funds-received screen, the real testimonial.

Personal Project · AI-Assisted Build

Voodoo Village · Weekend Timetable

Voodoo Village is a real festival: Grimbergen, Belgium, 11–13 September 2026, ten stages, dozens of acts across a weekend. I vibe-coded a personal timetable app for it with Claude: a live now-playing view, full-weekend search, and a clash-aware plan, built from the festival's own published lineup.

Personal project Built with Claude Open the app ↗

The Original

The festival publishes its timetable as a single dense poster image, one per day, like the one above, ten stages packed into a grid, meant to be downloaded and zoomed into rather than read standing in a field. No search, no sense of what's on right now, no way to build a plan across stages or catch two sets that overlap.

What I Built

A single-file web app, installable to a phone's home screen, that turns the same lineup data into something usable on the day:

  • Now: a live view of what's playing on every stage this minute, in Brussels time
  • Grid: the full day as a scrollable timeline across all ten stages
  • Stages: browse set by set, with artist bios and Spotify/SoundCloud/Instagram links where I could find them
  • Mine: star sets to build a personal plan; it flags overlaps and shows the free time between stages
  • Crew: an opt-in check-in so friends can see which stage everyone's at, off by default until it's wired to a backend

Try It

This is the real app below, not a mockup: switch tabs, star a set, see the plan update.

This isn't client work; it's a weekend side build for myself and whoever else is going. I'm including it because it's the clearest, fastest proof of the AI-assisted workflow the rest of this portfolio talks about: idea to a working, installable tool in an afternoon, not a sprint.

Personal Project · AI-Assisted Concept

Subsurface Intelligence Dashboard

A concept dashboard for monitoring borehole depth and contamination trend across a site, built after interviewing with GroundIQ (a Fugro venture), not a submission to their process, but a personal exploration of their product domain, vibe-coded with Claude.

Personal concept Built with Claude React / Tailwind, then rebuilt standalone

Why This Exists

During a GroundIQ interview process, I was given a collaborative exercise scoped as a verbal discussion, not a coding task: deliberately no code, no hi-fi design. Afterwards, I wanted to actually sit with their domain (ground risk and subsurface data) and see what a working interface for it could look like. This is that: a self-directed concept, not an interview deliverable.

The Domain

GroundIQ (Fugro) combines geophysical scanning and geotechnical data with AI analytics to de-risk ground conditions for large infrastructure projects, catching problems before they become budget overruns. I picked a narrower, concrete slice of that: a dashboard for tracking individual borehole readings and flagging which sites need attention.

What I Built

  • A card and map view of every monitored site, with contamination level surfaced at a glance through color coding
  • A detail panel per site with a contamination trend chart across recent samples and a contextual recommendation (routine cycle vs. flag for re-testing)
  • Filtering by risk level, search by site ID, and sorting by depth, risk, or sample recency
  • A self-contained schematic map view plotting sites by relative coordinates, colour-coded the same way as the cards

Try It

Real, working demo below: filter, search, switch to the map view, click a site to see its trend.

Honest Framing

Sample data only: coordinates, depths, and contamination readings are illustrative, not from a real survey. This is here to show how I think about an unfamiliar, technical domain and turn it into an interface fast, not as a claim about GroundIQ's actual product or process.

UX Design

Redesign · Web & Mobile for eir.ie

Eir is an Irish telecom e-commerce platform that wanted to broaden its services to elderly users, helping them manage bill payment and everyday account tasks online. The existing site wasn't built with this audience in mind, and it showed: low enthusiasm for digital bill pay and self-service.

Senior UI/UX Designer 3-month engagement Fully remote research (COVID-19) eir.ie ↗

Challenges & Goals

  • Usability: an intuitive, navigable site for users with limited digital experience.
  • Accessibility: designing for varying digital literacy and physical impairments, like reduced vision or dexterity.
  • Engagement: a design that motivates elderly users to actually use online services, not just tolerates them.
  • Time constraint: a three-month window to design and ship.
  • Remote collaboration: research, interviews, and testing all had to run remotely under COVID-19 restrictions.

Process

  1. Research & discoveryStakeholder meetings to align on business requirements, plus remote interviews with a diverse group of elderly users via Lookback and competitive analysis, to ground the approach in real needs rather than assumptions.
  2. Ideation & wireframingVirtual brainstorming sessions with the design team, then low-fidelity wireframes focused on simplicity and clear flow, iteratively refined against stakeholder and early user feedback.
  3. Prototyping & testingHigh-fidelity prototypes taken into remote usability testing sessions; results analyzed for usability issues, preferences, and areas to improve before build.
  4. Implementation & handoffA detailed technical specification for the development team, close collaboration through the build, and final adjustments driven by developer feedback and further user testing.

Research in Practice

The questionnaire was structured into sections for both desktop and mobile flows, run separately so each context got its own read on the experience. Task flows were documented step by step, for example a SIM card activation/registration flow and an Amazon Prime Video offer redemption flow, so engineering had zero ambiguity about what "done" looked like.

Design Philosophy

"Think, Make, and Check": understand the purpose, the audience, and the business objective; build the design; then test it against those goals. Every decision, down to the color of a button, was weighed against business guidelines and user needs. My role was to serve as the interpreter between the two.

Updated Prototype

Following interviews and in-depth analysis, I built out a high-fidelity prototype in Figma covering both mobile and desktop: bill breakdown, plan details, help & support, and account settings like changing a PIN.

Handoff Details

A full handoff file was created in Google Slides for developers, as per the client's request, covering IA, screen-by-screen flows for mobile and desktop, and edge cases as well as happy paths: panels that lazy-load with a progress spinner when data is slow, and a personalized greeting that adapts to what's known about the customer at load time, showing their name once it resolves, a friendly generic greeting if there's a delay.

Outcome

Delivered a redesigned, accessible web and mobile experience plus a full developer handoff package within the three-month window, shaped directly by interviews with the platform's most under-served user group rather than by internal assumptions about what "simple" means.

ROAR Platform for RiskOptics

The RiskOptics ROAR Platform gives compliance and security teams the ability to see, understand, and act on IT and cyber risk, automate compliance work, and communicate impact to leadership.

Senior UI/UX Designer Riskoptics (ZenGRC) Dec 2022 – Dec 2023 · US Remote

The Challenge

The challenge was to build a new UX & Product vision. The fields and features I needed to build were: inventory of vendors & services, third-party risk management, risk questionnaires, inventory of policies, inventory of people (employees & contractors), the assessment for all of the above, identifying high-risk areas, and reusing evidence.

My Role

I was responsible for rebuilding the UX and product vision based on business requirements, user research, information architecture, and platform capacity. That meant leading a full redesign of the analytics platform end to end, from requirements through delivery, for a B2B SaaS audience managing compliance workflows: audits, frameworks, findings, and control implementation tracking.

Planning & Coordination

I collaborated with another lead UX/UI designer within the team. My responsibilities included working with business requirements, collaborating with the product and development teams, planning and estimating UX and UI activities, and making presentations and giving demos to stakeholders. Evidence & Policy Review

Two of the workflows I designed inside the platform: attaching and tracking evidence against a control, and routing a policy through review before it's approved.

Beyond the Product

I also served as a key stakeholder representing user needs in the build of an internal ERP system, working directly with engineering leadership, extending UX involvement beyond the customer-facing product into the internal tooling that supported it.

Outcome

A simplified, more legible compliance workflow for a B2B SaaS audience: clearer requirement status, audit calendars, findings, and control implementations, redesigned from the ground up around how compliance teams actually work.

RunOn · Mobile App for Running

RunOn's goal is to make running fun and interesting: the client wanted to engage runners by streaming stories whose plot is tied to the runner's heartbeat, turning a run into a chapter instead of just a workout.

UX / Product Design Sketch · InVision · Zeplin

The Challenge

The biggest challenge for the project was sending users' heart rate to the app and making sure it would influence the storyline.

Results

We connected the Apple Watch heart rate monitor to the app to get live heart rate data. That, in turn, connected to our storyline database and allowed the next part of the storyline to be chosen by the user's heart rate range.

What I Designed

  • Activity feed: recent and past runs, each tied to a story and its chapter progress.
  • Live run screen: heartbeat-linked story pacing with pause, resume, and heartbeat-range selection.
  • Post-run recap: distance, calories, and experience earned, with a share action back into the app's social feed.

Additional: Apple Watch

I also developed an additional design option and a variation for the watch, extending the same story-driven run experience to a smaller screen.

Planning & Coordination

I collaborated with another UX/UI designer within the team. My responsibilities included working with business requirements, collaborating with the product and development teams, planning and estimating UX and UI activities, and making presentations and giving demos to stakeholders.

UX Design

UX for three.ie

A Customer Journey Map (CJM) is a method used to organize and visualize the path a user follows to achieve a positive outcome within a product. CJMs shed light on user pain points and help the team resolve them.

UX/UI Designer CJM · Heuristic Evaluation

My Role

I undertook the responsibility of crafting UX and design solutions by aligning business requirements, conducting user research, considering information architecture, and factoring in platform capabilities and capacity.

How I Built the CJM

I enriched the Customer Journey Map by incorporating: Objectives: the specific goals users aim to achieve; Actions: the sequence of steps users take; Contact Points: the pivotal touchpoints for gathering insight; Pain Points: moments of frustration or inconvenience; Emotions: users' emotional responses at key steps; and Opportunities: recommendations to improve the experience.

Choice of Tools

Working remotely, I opted to use Miro. While CJMs are often built in Excel or spreadsheets, Miro's collaborative environment, digital stickers, and team interaction capabilities suited this project better.

Additionally: Heuristic Evaluation

I ran a Heuristic Evaluation, assessing the live product against a comprehensive set of usability guidelines to identify issues and propose solutions: for example, checking whether users are clearly notified of changes in their journey, like unavailable items in a product card.

Outcome

After developing CJMs across three epics, the team had a comprehensive overview of critical user pathways within the service. We gained valuable insight into the product from the user's perspective, assessed current pain points, and identified concrete opportunities to improve the experience.
